feature: A walk can rest the pointer on something
summary: A scripted walk can now put the pointer on a control and the app reacts the way it does for a hand, so everything the app does on hover is testable for the first time. The line at the foot of the canvas is the first thing proved: resting on its button keeps it from leaving, walking away lets it go.
setup: Nothing to turn on. This is walk machinery, so the way to see it is to run a walk: Scripts/playtest.sh Scripts/playtest/notice-waits-under-the-pointer-walk.json --no-build. The picture below came out of that run.

try.do: Run Scripts/playtest.sh Scripts/playtest/notice-waits-under-the-pointer-walk.json --no-build and watch it finish green in about twenty seconds.
Read the log line for step 11: it says the pointer came to rest on "Read the Words" and where that button actually was.
try.shotNote: Photographed while the Mac was locked. The window is the real one, drawn and driven normally, with two known costs: colours can read dimmed, and a tutorial card does not draw at all because the login window is over it.

try.do: Open the walk and see that it aims by NAME, not by numbers: { "do": "move", "control": "Read the Words" }.
Break the app on purpose: make EditorState.holdCanvasNotice return straight away, rebuild the probe, run the walk again. It fails at step 12 and names the control to rest on.
Put it back, then read "What resting the pointer on something proves" in docs/design/playtest-harness.md for which steps move the pointer and what the technique can and cannot prove.
Run Scripts/test.sh and watch PlaytestHoverIsReachableTests: it fails the build's tests if anyone writes a bare .onHover again.

evaluate: Is "rest the pointer on the control called X" the way you would want to write this in a walk, or would you rather point at coordinates?
The walk proves everything that happens BECAUSE of a hover, but not SwiftUI's own delivery of the crossing. Is that the right trade, given no synthetic event on this Mac can do the second?
Twenty hovers in the app were rewritten as playtestHover. Does a test that fails on a bare .onHover feel like a useful guard or like a nuisance?
A wait can now be put back on the clock for a walk about a timer. Should anything else in the set be spending real seconds?
rough: A pointer resting on a region whose view is COVERED by something else still counts as resting on it. Nothing in the app hits this today because the overlapping surfaces are at different places, but a walk that rested on a spot under a panel would get a hover a hand would not.
The screen was locked for this whole task, so nothing here was seen by eye. Every claim comes from the walk and from real window captures taken under the lock.

hover now joins the steps a lock cannot touch: six tooltip walks were being refused on a locked Mac and four of them now run unforced (the other two are refused for a menuShot and a step nobody has watched yet). That was proved by forcing them first and reading the result, not by assuming.
